topics.title: Introduction to Costing Methods
explain: Costing methods are chosen based on industry type and management requirements.
Industries are broadly categorized into job work industries and continuous/process industries.
Job work concerns execute unique orders strictly based on customer specifications.
Job work industries use Job Costing, Contract Costing, and Batch Costing.
Continuous or process industries produce uniform, mass-manufactured standardized products.
Process industries use Process Costing, Single Output (Unit) Costing, and Operating Costing.

flow.title: Selecting Method of Costing by Industry Type
steps: Identify if Special Order or Continuous
If Custom Orders, Choose Job Work Costing
If Mass Uniform Goods, Choose Process Costing
Ascertain Cost per Unit or Lot

topics.example: A custom furniture shop uses Job Costing for each unique custom table, whereas a cement factory uses Unit Costing for standardized bags of cement.
remember: Job Work = unique customer specifications (Job, Contract, Batch Costing).
Continuous Production = mass standardized goods (Process, Unit Costing).
mistakes: Confusing costing methods (e.g., Job or Unit Costing) with costing techniques (e.g., Marginal or Standard Costing).

quiz.q: Which costing method is applied when goods are manufactured against unique customer specifications?
quiz.why: Job work concerns execute unique orders to customer specification using Job Costing.

quiz.q: Which of the following industries typically uses continuous or process type costing?
quiz.why: Pharmaceuticals involve continuous mass production of standardized identical goods.

topics.title: Unit Costing and Cost Collection Procedure
explain: Unit Costing (or Single/Output Costing) applies when output is identical and consumes identical costs.
It is used in single-product industries like cement, paper, steel, mining, and breweries.
Cost per unit is calculated as Total Cost of Production divided by Number of Units Produced.
Material costs are accumulated from Material Requisition Notes.
Direct labour costs are collected from job time cards or time sheets.
Normal defective work within limits is charged to total output; abnormal defective loss is written off to Costing P&L.

flow.title: Unit Cost Accumulation Process
steps: Collect Raw Material via Requisition Notes
Track Direct Labour via Time Cards

topics.example: A paper mill calculates total monthly production cost of Rs 7,68,000 for 10,000 units, arriving at a works cost of Rs 76.80 per unit.
remember: Cost per unit = Total Cost of Production / No. of units produced.
Normal defective loss = charged to entire output.
Abnormal defective loss = written off to Costing Profit & Loss Account.
mistakes: Charging abnormal defective or rectification costs to good units instead of writing them off to Costing Profit & Loss Account.

quiz.q: What is the formula for calculating cost per unit under Unit Costing?
o: Total Cost of Production / Number of units produced
Direct Material Cost / Number of units sold
Total Sales Revenue / Number of units produced
quiz.why: Unit cost is found by dividing total cost of production by total units produced.

quiz.q: How is the cost of defective work handled if it exceeds normal established limits?
o: Written off to Costing Profit and Loss Account
quiz.why: Loss or rectification cost beyond normal limits is treated as abnormal and written off to Costing P&L.

topics.title: Batch Costing and Costing Procedure
explain: Batch Costing is a form of specific order costing where goods are produced in predetermined lots called batches.
The cost object is a batch of identical items rather than a single individual unit.
Minimum fixed expenses, such as machine setup and supervision, occur each time a batch is initiated.
A unique batch number is assigned to collect direct materials, direct labour, and absorbed overheads.
Total cost of the batch is divided by the number of units in the batch to find unit cost.

flow.title: Batch Costing Execution Steps
steps: Log Direct Labour Time on batch

topics.example: A bakery bakes muffins in batches of 50. Oven setup costs (Rs 150) and direct inputs are tracked per batch of 50 to find the cost per muffin.
remember: Batch Costing cost object = The Batch.
Setup costs are incurred each time a batch is run, regardless of batch size.
mistakes: Treating setup cost as a variable cost per unit rather than a fixed cost per batch setup.

quiz.q: In Batch Costing, what serves as the primary cost object?
o: The entire factory output for a year
quiz.why: Under batch costing, the cost object for cost determination is a batch.

quiz.q: Which of the following costs is incurred each time a batch is started, irrespective of the number of units in it?
quiz.why: Machine setup is a minimum expenditure required every time a batch production run is initiated.

topics.title: Economic Batch Quantity (EBQ)
explain: EBQ is the optimum batch size that minimizes total setup costs and inventory carrying costs.
Increasing batch size lowers setup cost per unit (fewer setups) but increases inventory holding cost.
Decreasing batch size lowers inventory holding cost but increases annual setup costs.
Formula: EBQ = Square Root of [ (2 * D * S) / C ].
Where D = Annual demand for the product, S = Setup cost per batch, and C = Carrying cost per unit per annum.

flow.title: EBQ Computation & Optimization Flow
steps: Calculate Carrying Cost per Unit p.a. (C)

topics.example: If annual demand D = 48,000 bearings, setup cost S = Rs 3,200, and annual carrying cost C = Rs 12 per unit, EBQ = sqrt((2 x 48,000 x 3,200) / 12) = 5,060 units.
remember: C must be Carrying Cost per unit PER ANNUM.
mistakes: Plugging monthly demand or monthly carrying cost directly into the EBQ formula without converting to annual values.

quiz.q: Economic Batch Quantity is the batch size where:
o: Setup cost is equal to total sales
Total cost of setup and carrying cost is minimized
Production run size is at maximum plant capacity
quiz.why: EBQ optimizes the trade-off between setup costs and inventory holding costs to achieve minimum total cost.

quiz.q: In the EBQ formula sqrt(2DS/C), what does 'C' stand for?
o: Carrying cost per unit per annum
quiz.why: 'C' represents the inventory carrying cost per unit per annum.

topics.title: Difference Between Job Costing and Batch Costing
explain: Job Costing is applied to non-standard, unique goods made to order.
Batch Costing is applied to homogeneous goods produced in continuous lots.
In Job Costing, cost is determined separately for each distinct job.
In Batch Costing, cost is calculated in aggregate for the whole batch and then averaged per unit.
Jobs are unique and independent; units in a batch are uniform and lack individual identity.

flow.title: Distinguishing Job Costing vs Batch Costing
steps: If Yes -> Apply Job Costing per Job
If Yes -> Apply Batch Costing per Batch

topics.example: Building a custom bridge uses Job Costing because each order is unique; manufacturing 10,000 identical pens uses Batch Costing.
remember: Job Costing = unique job, cost per job.
Batch Costing = homogeneous lot, aggregate batch cost divided by units.
mistakes: Assuming units produced within the same batch have unique individual costs.

quiz.q: Which characteristic correctly describes Batch Costing compared to Job Costing?
o: Each item produced is unique and independent
Homogeneous products are produced in continuous lots
Cost is determined separately for each individual item
It is only used for long-term construction projects
quiz.why: Batch costing applies to homogeneous products produced in lots.

quiz.q: How is unit cost arrived at in Batch Costing?
o: By tracking specific costs for each unit separately
By dividing total aggregate batch cost by the number of units in the batch
By adding setup cost to unit selling price
By taking a fixed percentage of total sales value
quiz.why: Costs are accumulated for the entire batch and then divided by batch units to get unit cost.
